Solve the equation below. \[63=(x+3)\cdot 9\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[63=(x+3)\cdot 9\] Divide both sides of the equation by 9.

\[7=x+3\]

Subtract 3 from both sides of the equation.

\[4=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=4\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 4 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[63\stackrel{?}{=}((4)+3)\cdot 9\]

\[63 \stackrel{?}{=} 7\cdot 9\]

\[63 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 63\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=4\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[34=8 x-6\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[34=8 x-6\] Add 6 to both sides of the equation.

\[40=8 x\]

Divide both sides of the equation by 8.

\[5=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=5\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 5 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[34\stackrel{?}{=}8 (5)-6\]

\[34 \stackrel{?}{=} 40-6\]

\[34 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 34\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=5\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[33=4 x+5\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[33=4 x+5\] Subtract 5 from both sides of the equation.

\[28=4 x\]

Divide both sides of the equation by 4.

\[7=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=7\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 7 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[33\stackrel{?}{=}4 (7)+5\]

\[33 \stackrel{?}{=} 28+5\]

\[33 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 33\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=7\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[60=(x+7)\cdot 6\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[60=(x+7)\cdot 6\] Divide both sides of the equation by 6.

\[10=x+7\]

Subtract 7 from both sides of the equation.

\[3=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=3\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 3 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[60\stackrel{?}{=}((3)+7)\cdot 6\]

\[60 \stackrel{?}{=} 10\cdot 6\]

\[60 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 60\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=3\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[3=\frac{x-3}{2}\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[3=\frac{x-3}{2}\] Multiply both sides of the equation by 2.

\[6=x-3\]

Add 3 to both sides of the equation.

\[9=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=9\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 9 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[3\stackrel{?}{=}\frac{(9)-3}{2}\]

\[3 \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{6}{2}\]

\[3 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 3\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=9\) is a solution to the equation.

On the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) exists the point \((100,10)\) because \(10=\sqrt{100}\).

We can transform the square-root function horizontally and vertically to create a new curve defined by the equation below:

\[y=2\cdot \sqrt{\frac{x-8}{5}}-4\]

Find this curve's corresponding point by finding the value of \(x\) that makes the radicand equal to 100, and then find the \(y\) value by evaluating the right side of the equation. Express that point using parentheses, a comma separator, and no spaces. For example, type (18,-5) for the point \((18,-5)\).

Set the radicand (the argument of the square-root function) equal to 100.

\[\frac{x-8}{5}=100\]

Solve the two-step (or maybe three-step) linear equation.

\[x=508\]

Plug \(x=508\) into equation.

\[y=2\cdot \sqrt{\frac{(508)-8}{5}}-4\]

Simplify the radicand.

\[y=2\cdot \sqrt{100}-4\]

Evaluate the radical.

\[y=2\cdot 10-4\]

Evaluate the right side using PEMDAS.

\[y=16\]

So, the corresponding point on the transformed curve is (508,16).

On the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) exists the point \((16,4)\) because \(4=\sqrt{16}\).

We can transform the square-root function horizontally and vertically to create a new curve defined by the equation below:

\[y=5\cdot\left(\sqrt{3 x+4}-10\right)\]

Find this curve's corresponding point by finding the value of \(x\) that makes the radicand equal to 16, and then find the \(y\) value by evaluating the right side of the equation. Express that point using parentheses, a comma separator, and no spaces. For example, type (18,-5) for the point \((18,-5)\).

Set the radicand (the argument of the square-root function) equal to 16.

\[3 x+4=16\]

Solve the two-step (or maybe three-step) linear equation.

\[x=4\]

Plug \(x=4\) into equation.

\[y=5\cdot\left(\sqrt{3 (4)+4}-10\right)\]

Simplify the radicand.

\[y=5\cdot\left(\sqrt{16}-10\right)\]

Evaluate the radical.

\[y=5\cdot\left(4-10\right)\]

Evaluate the right side using PEMDAS.

\[y=-30\]

So, the corresponding point on the transformed curve is (4,-30).

On the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) exists the point \((36,6)\) because \(6=\sqrt{36}\).

We can transform the square-root function horizontally and vertically to create a new curve defined by the equation below:

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{x}{6}+5}}{3}-4\]

Find this curve's corresponding point by finding the value of \(x\) that makes the radicand equal to 36, and then find the \(y\) value by evaluating the right side of the equation. Express that point using parentheses, a comma separator, and no spaces. For example, type (18,-5) for the point \((18,-5)\).

Set the radicand (the argument of the square-root function) equal to 36.

\[\frac{x}{6}+5=36\]

Solve the two-step (or maybe three-step) linear equation.

\[x=186\]

Plug \(x=186\) into equation.

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{(186)}{6}+5}}{3}-4\]

Simplify the radicand.

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{36}}{3}-4\]

Evaluate the radical.

\[y=\frac{6}{3}-4\]

Evaluate the right side using PEMDAS.

\[y=-2\]

So, the corresponding point on the transformed curve is (186,-2).

On the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) exists the point \((49,7)\) because \(7=\sqrt{49}\).

We can transform the square-root function horizontally and vertically to create a new curve defined by the equation below:

\[y=-5\cdot\left(\sqrt{-2 x+7}-8\right)\]

Find this curve's corresponding point by finding the value of \(x\) that makes the radicand equal to 49, and then find the \(y\) value by evaluating the right side of the equation. Express that point using parentheses, a comma separator, and no spaces. For example, type (18,-5) for the point \((18,-5)\).

Set the radicand (the argument of the square-root function) equal to 49.

\[-2 x+7=49\]

Solve the two-step (or maybe three-step) linear equation.

\[x=-21\]

Plug \(x=-21\) into equation.

\[y=-5\cdot\left(\sqrt{-2 (-21)+7}-8\right)\]

Simplify the radicand.

\[y=-5\cdot\left(\sqrt{49}-8\right)\]

Evaluate the radical.

\[y=-5\cdot\left(7-8\right)\]

Evaluate the right side using PEMDAS.

\[y=5\]

So, the corresponding point on the transformed curve is (-21,5).

On the curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) exists the point \((16,4)\) because \(4=\sqrt{16}\).

We can transform the square-root function horizontally and vertically to create a new curve defined by the equation below:

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{-2 x-8}+5}{3}\]

Find this curve's corresponding point by finding the value of \(x\) that makes the radicand equal to 16, and then find the \(y\) value by evaluating the right side of the equation. Express that point using parentheses, a comma separator, and no spaces. For example, type (18,-5) for the point \((18,-5)\).

Set the radicand (the argument of the square-root function) equal to 16.

\[-2 x-8=16\]

Solve the two-step (or maybe three-step) linear equation.

\[x=-12\]

Plug \(x=-12\) into equation.

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{-2 (-12)-8}+5}{3}\]

Simplify the radicand.

\[y=\frac{\sqrt{16}+5}{3}\]

Evaluate the radical.

\[y=\frac{4+5}{3}\]

Evaluate the right side using PEMDAS.

\[y=3\]

So, the corresponding point on the transformed curve is (-12,3).

The quadratic polynomial \(p(x)\) is defined below.

\[p(x)~=~x^{2}-{12}x+{27}\]

Which two linear polynomials are factors of \(p(x)\)?

You can get this by guessing and checking. Eventually you might guess the following:

\[p(x) ~=~ (x-{3})\cdot(x-{9})\]

You can check by using polynomial multiplication (in this case you can use the FOIL method).

* \(x\) \(-3\)
\(x\) \(x^2\) \({-3}x\)
\(-9\) \({-9}x\) \(27\)

\[p(x) ~=~ x^{2}-{3}x-{9}x+{27}\]

\[p(x) ~=~ x^{2}-{12}x+{27}\]

After you've done this a few hundred times, you'll notice that you wanted two numbers that added to give -12 and multiplied to give 27. So, you start thinking of factor pairs of 27 until you find a pair that sums to -12. You will see that below I've listed all factor pairs of 27, along with the corresponding polynomials in factored and expanded forms.

Factor pairs of 27 Factored polynomial Expanded polynomial
1 and 27 \((x+{1})\cdot (x+{27})\) \(x^{2}+{28}x+{27}\)
-1 and -27 \((x-{1})\cdot (x-{27})\) \(x^{2}-{28}x+{27}\)
3 and 9 \((x+{3})\cdot (x+{9})\) \(x^{2}+{12}x+{27}\)
-3 and -9 \((x-{3})\cdot (x-{9})\) \(x^{2}-{12}x+{27}\)

And, so, \(x^{2}-{12}x+{27}\) is an equivalent expression to \((x-{3})\cdot(x-{9})\), which is also equivalent to \((x-{9})\cdot(x-{3})\).

Solve the following equation:

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{5})^2-13~=~-8\]

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{5})^2-13~=~-8\]

First, add 13 to both sides.

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{5})^2~=~5\]

Second, multiply both sides by 20.

\[(x-{5})^2~=~100\]

Undo the squaring. Remember the plus-minus symbol!

\[x-{5}~=~\pm10\]

Add 5 to both sides.

\[x~=~5\pm10\]

So the two solutions are \(x=15\) and \(x=-5\).

Solve the following equation:

\[\frac{1}{3}(x+{5})^2+9~=~21\]

\[\frac{1}{3}(x+{5})^2+9~=~21\]

First, subtract 9 from both sides.

\[\frac{1}{3}(x+{5})^2~=~12\]

Second, multiply both sides by 3.

\[(x+{5})^2~=~36\]

Undo the squaring. Remember the plus-minus symbol!

\[x+{5}~=~\pm6\]

Subtract 5 from both sides.

\[x~=~-5\pm6\]

So the two solutions are \(x=1\) and \(x=-11\).

Solve the following equation:

\[\frac{1}{12}(x-{4})^2+14~=~17\]

\[\frac{1}{12}(x-{4})^2+14~=~17\]

First, subtract 14 from both sides.

\[\frac{1}{12}(x-{4})^2~=~3\]

Second, multiply both sides by 12.

\[(x-{4})^2~=~36\]

Undo the squaring. Remember the plus-minus symbol!

\[x-{4}~=~\pm6\]

Add 4 to both sides.

\[x~=~4\pm6\]

So the two solutions are \(x=10\) and \(x=-2\).

Solve the following equation:

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{7})^2-15~=~-10\]

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{7})^2-15~=~-10\]

First, add 15 to both sides.

\[\frac{1}{20}(x-{7})^2~=~5\]

Second, multiply both sides by 20.

\[(x-{7})^2~=~100\]

Undo the squaring. Remember the plus-minus symbol!

\[x-{7}~=~\pm10\]

Add 7 to both sides.

\[x~=~7\pm10\]

So the two solutions are \(x=17\) and \(x=-3\).

Solve the following equation:

\[\frac{1}{3}(x-{10})^2-16~=~11\]

\[\frac{1}{3}(x-{10})^2-16~=~11\]

First, add 16 to both sides.

\[\frac{1}{3}(x-{10})^2~=~27\]

Second, multiply both sides by 3.

\[(x-{10})^2~=~81\]

Undo the squaring. Remember the plus-minus symbol!

\[x-{10}~=~\pm9\]

Add 10 to both sides.

\[x~=~10\pm9\]

So the two solutions are \(x=19\) and \(x=1\).

Consider the following product of linear binomials:

\[({5}x-{8})(x-{9})\]

When the expression is expanded and like terms are combined, an equivalent expression can be expressed in standard form:

\[ax^2+bx+c\]

where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are integers.

  • What is the value of \(b\)?

You could use the box method.


Or, you can FOIL...


Either way, you should first get \[{5}x^{2}-{45}x-{8}x+{72}\]

And, after combining like terms, you should get \[{5}x^{2}-{53}x+{72}\]

Thus, \(a=5\) and \(b=-53\) and \(c=72\). This question specifically asked for the value of \(b\), so the answer is \(-53\).

Consider the following product of linear binomials:

\[(-x+{6})({-2}x+{7})\]

When the expression is expanded and like terms are combined, an equivalent expression can be expressed in standard form:

\[ax^2+bx+c\]

where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are integers.

  • What is the value of \(b\)?

You could use the box method.


Or, you can FOIL...


Either way, you should first get \[{2}x^{2}-{7}x-{12}x+{42}\]

And, after combining like terms, you should get \[{2}x^{2}-{19}x+{42}\]

Thus, \(a=2\) and \(b=-19\) and \(c=42\). This question specifically asked for the value of \(b\), so the answer is \(-19\).

Consider the quadratic expression shown in standard form:

\[{5}x^{2}+{38}x+{21}\]

In factored form, the expression can be represented as the product of two factors. What are those factors?

Rewrite the given quadratic expression:

\[{5}x^{2}+{38}x+{21}\]

Set up a box with what you know... Notice that the leading (quadratic) coefficient, \(a=5\), is prime. This allows us to be more confident in how this expression factors.

You can get this by guessing and checking. To make a smart guess, find a pair of integers that multiply to get \(21\), and use those...

Eventually, because \((3)\cdot(7)=21\), you will guess the following factored form:

\[({5}x+{3})\cdot(x+{7})\]

And you will check it with a box to see that it works.

\[{5}x^{2}+{35}x+{3}x+{21}\]

Combine like terms.

\[{5}x^{2}+{38}x+{21}\]

So it worked! (Because it matches the given standard-form expression.) Thus, in factored form, the expression is:

\[({5}x+{3})\cdot(x+{7})\]

And, the two factors are \(({5}x+{3})\) and \((x+{7})\)

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x+{9})^2~=~36\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-6\) and \(6\) produce \(36\).

\[(x+{9})^2~=~36\]

\[x+{9}~=~\pm6\]

\[x~=~-9\pm6\]

So the two solutions are \(x=-3\) and \(x=-15\).

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x-{5})^2~=~16\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-4\) and \(4\) produce \(16\).

\[(x-{5})^2~=~16\]

\[x-{5}~=~\pm4\]

\[x~=~5\pm4\]

So the two solutions are \(x=9\) and \(x=1\).

\[(x+{5})^2~=~16\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-4\) and \(4\) produce \(16\).

\[(x+{5})^2~=~16\]

\[x+{5}~=~\pm4\]

\[x~=~-5\pm4\]

So the two solutions are \(x=-1\) and \(x=-9\).

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x-{5})^2~=~64\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-8\) and \(8\) produce \(64\).

\[(x-{5})^2~=~64\]

\[x-{5}~=~\pm8\]

\[x~=~5\pm8\]

So the two solutions are \(x=13\) and \(x=-3\).

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x-{8})^2~=~25\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-5\) and \(5\) produce \(25\).

\[(x-{8})^2~=~25\]

\[x-{8}~=~\pm5\]

\[x~=~8\pm5\]

So the two solutions are \(x=13\) and \(x=3\).

Find the remainder when \(6x³-41x²+27x+14\) is divided by \(x-6\).

Fill out the polynomial long division shown below to divide \(6x³-41x²+27x+14\) by \(x-6\).

6x² -5x -3
x -6 6x³ -41x² +27x +14
\(-(\) 6x³ -36x² \()\)
-5x² +27x
\(-(\) -5x² +30x \()\)
-3x +14
\(-(\) -3x +18 \()\)
-4

Thus, the following identity holds true for all values of \(x\) (but \(x\ne 6\)):

\[\frac{6x^3-41x^2+27x+14}{x-6}~=~6x^2-5x-3+\frac{-4}{x-6}\]

And the remainder is \(-4\).

Find the remainder when \(9x³+28x²-29x+6\) is divided by \(x+4\).

Fill out the polynomial long division shown below to divide \(9x³+28x²-29x+6\) by \(x+4\).

9x² -8x +3
x +4 9x³ +28x² -29x +6
\(-(\) 9x³ +36x² \()\)
-8x² -29x
\(-(\) -8x² -32x \()\)
3x +6
\(-(\) 3x +12 \()\)
-6

Thus, the following identity holds true for all values of \(x\) (but \(x\ne -4\)):

\[\frac{9x^3+28x^2-29x+6}{x+4}~=~9x^2-8x+3+\frac{-6}{x+4}\]

And the remainder is \(-6\).

Find the remainder when \(3x³-17x²-62x+54\) is divided by \(x-8\).

Fill out the polynomial long division shown below to divide \(3x³-17x²-62x+54\) by \(x-8\).

3x² +7x -6
x -8 3x³ -17x² -62x +54
\(-(\) 3x³ -24x² \()\)
7x² -62x
\(-(\) 7x² -56x \()\)
-6x +54
\(-(\) -6x +48 \()\)
6

Thus, the following identity holds true for all values of \(x\) (but \(x\ne 8\)):

\[\frac{3x^3-17x^2-62x+54}{x-8}~=~3x^2+7x-6+\frac{6}{x-8}\]

And the remainder is \(6\).

Find the remainder when \(6x³-20x²-13x-9\) is divided by \(x-4\).

Fill out the polynomial long division shown below to divide \(6x³-20x²-13x-9\) by \(x-4\).

6x² +4x +3
x -4 6x³ -20x² -13x -9
\(-(\) 6x³ -24x² \()\)
4x² -13x
\(-(\) 4x² -16x \()\)
3x -9
\(-(\) 3x -12 \()\)
3

Thus, the following identity holds true for all values of \(x\) (but \(x\ne 4\)):

\[\frac{6x^3-20x^2-13x-9}{x-4}~=~6x^2+4x+3+\frac{3}{x-4}\]

And the remainder is \(3\).

Find the remainder when \(2x³+13x²+14x-26\) is divided by \(x+4\).

Fill out the polynomial long division shown below to divide \(2x³+13x²+14x-26\) by \(x+4\).

2x² +5x -6
x +4 2x³ +13x² +14x -26
\(-(\) 2x³ +8x² \()\)
5x² +14x
\(-(\) 5x² +20x \()\)
-6x -26
\(-(\) -6x -24 \()\)
-2

Thus, the following identity holds true for all values of \(x\) (but \(x\ne -4\)):

\[\frac{2x^3+13x^2+14x-26}{x+4}~=~2x^2+5x-6+\frac{-2}{x+4}\]

And the remainder is \(-2\).

Consider the shifted square-root function graphed below:


Which equation represents the plotted curve?

The parent function, \(y=\sqrt{x}\), has been shifted \(4\) units left and \(6\) units up.

The correct answer is \[y=\sqrt{x+4}+6\]

Notice the horizontal translation is counterintuitive. The horizontal coordinate transformation is the INVERSE of the argument expression, whereas the vertical coordinate transformation is simply the outer operations.

\[(a,b)~\to~(a-4,b+6)\]

where \((a,b)\) is a solution to the parent equation \(\sqrt{a}=b\). For example, \(\sqrt{0}=0\) or \(\sqrt{1}=1\) or \(\sqrt{4}=2\) or \(\sqrt{9}=3\)... Thus from curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to curve \(y=\sqrt{x+4}+6\), we have the following coordinate transformations:

\[(0,0) \to (-4,6)\] \[(1,1) \to (-3,7)\] \[(4,2) \to (0,8)\] \[(9,3) \to (5,9)\]

Notice the horizontal translation is counterintuitive. The horizontal coordinate transformation is the INVERSE of the argument expression, whereas the vertical coordinate transformation is simply the outer operations.

\[(a,b)~\to~(a-2,b+5)\]

where \((a,b)\) is a solution to the parent equation \(\sqrt{a}=b\). For example, \(\sqrt{0}=0\) or \(\sqrt{1}=1\) or \(\sqrt{4}=2\) or \(\sqrt{9}=3\)... Thus from curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to curve \(y=\sqrt{x+2}+5\), we have the following coordinate transformations:

\[(0,0) \to (-2,5)\] \[(1,1) \to (-1,6)\] \[(4,2) \to (2,7)\] \[(9,3) \to (7,8)\]

where \((a,b)\) is a solution to the parent equation \(\sqrt{a}=b\). For example, \(\sqrt{0}=0\) or \(\sqrt{1}=1\) or \(\sqrt{4}=2\) or \(\sqrt{9}=3\)... Thus from curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to curve \(y=\sqrt{x-3}+2\), we have the following coordinate transformations:

A rectangle's width is 2 meters shorter than its height. The area is 274 square meters. In meters, what is the height? (Answers should be accurate within \(\pm 0.1\) meters)

Let \(x\) represent the height. The width is \(x-{2}\). The area of a rectangle equals the product of height times width.

\[274~=~x\cdot (x-{2})\]

Distribute the multiplication of \(x\) to the terms in parentheses.

\[274~=~x^{2}-{2}x\]

Subtract 274 from both sides.

\[0~=~x^{2}-{2}x-{274}\]

Now the right side of the equation is in standard form. We can identify \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) in order to use the quadratic formula.

\[a=1\] \[b=-2\] \[c=-274\]

Remember the formula.

\[x~=~\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\]

Plug in the coefficients.

\[x~=~\frac{-(-2)\pm \sqrt{(-2)^2-4(1)(-274)}}{2(1)}\]

Simplify.

\[x~=~\frac{2\pm \sqrt{{4}+{1096}}}{2}\]

Simplify more.

\[x~=~\frac{2\pm \sqrt{1100}}{2}\]

Simplify more.

\[x~=~\frac{2\pm 10\sqrt{11}}{2}\]

Simplify more.\[x~=~1\pm 5\sqrt{11}\]

This (or, honestly, one of the earlier, less simplified expressions) can be put into a calculator to get the two possible values for \(x\) as decimal approximations. We are only interested in the positive solution.

\[x=17.583124\]

Consider the quadratic equation with a standard-form quadratic expression on the left side and zero on the right side.

\[x^{2}+{7}x+{12}~=~0\]

Find all solutions.

Factor the left-side expression.

\[(x+{4}) (x+{3})=0\]

The zero-product property tells us that if a product equals 0, then at least one of the factors of the product equals 0. In this case, we know the product of \((x+{4})\) and \((x+{3})\) equals zero. This means to satisfy the equation either \(x+{4}\) equals zero or \(x+{3}\) equals zero. Solve each of these using addition or subtraction.

  • First solution: \[x+{4}=0\] \[x=-4\]

  • Second solution: \[x+{3}=0\] \[x=-3\]

Thus, the two solutions are \(x=-4\) and \(x=-3\).

\[(x+{5}) (x-{9})=0\]

The zero-product property tells us that if a product equals 0, then at least one of the factors of the product equals 0. In this case, we know the product of \((x+{5})\) and \((x-{9})\) equals zero. This means to satisfy the equation either \(x+{5}\) equals zero or \(x-{9}\) equals zero. Solve each of these using addition or subtraction.

  • First solution: \[x+{5}=0\] \[x=-5\]

  • Second solution: \[x-{9}=0\] \[x=9\]

Thus, the two solutions are \(x=-5\) and \(x=9\).
